We have already seen multiple examples demonstrating that granting the Meta Muse app on Mac "Full Disk Access" is an extremely terrible idea, and now another major privacy issue has been exposed: Muse has been found to be analyzing your communications with everyone in your life on an hourly basis.

It is reasonable for Apple to express concern over this development; in a blog post, the company stated that it would introduce additional controls for the "Full Disk Access" feature — which has been the root cause of this issue.

Meta's Muse app has made the situation urgent

Meta recently launched the personal AI agent assistant Muse for iPhone and Mac. Although granting a Meta app full access to all your Apple devices is clearly not something to be encouraged, the app has nonetheless quickly surged to the top of the App Store charts.

Predictably, the situation quickly spiraled severely out of control, and there has been no improvement to date — *Wired* reported that security researcher Karan Joshi discovered Meta had directed Muse to collect all the data needed to build a complete map of all your relationships.

One of Muse's instructions appears to give it the capability to "create profile pages for every person in the user's life." This hourly procedure involves gathering data on family members, partners, friends, colleagues, "collaborators," and people you "track," with the instructions stating: "where they live, what they do for work, what topics they frequently discuss (moving house, joint savings goals)." It also specifies that the model can record "important dates" such as birthdays or anniversaries. A person's history could include background details like "a March trip, a resolved argument, last week's milestone."

Apple tightens "Full Disk Access"

You might think the prompt requesting "Full Disk Access" on Mac is clear enough, but that is evidently not the case. Even savvy users have granted this sweeping permission without fully realizing how dangerous such a step is.

Apple said this feature was originally designed for backup apps, but developers have subsequently used it for broader applications, including AI assistants. The company indicated its intention to "introduce additional controls" to ensure users fully understand what they are doing when granting this permission.

What Apple must and should do

Apple describes this step as "critical," and I fully agree. When the existing permission request clearly fails to adequately convey the gravity of granting this access, Apple must ensure that users truly understand what they are permitting.

I would very much like to see clearer, more explicit wording warning people not to do this unless they are certain they understand the consequences. Something along the lines of:

Basically, more stern wording cannot be too strong. I would also welcome a one-time confirmation for apps that have already been granted this permission.

Peter — most-liked comment

Although I find it occasionally annoying when Apple asks me whether I still want to give an app access to my location, I do appreciate this design. There have been times when I discovered I no longer wanted a particular app to have that degree of access. It also reminds me to periodically think about which apps might be using my location data.

However, Apple absolutely must not repeat the debacle it had with screen recording in macOS Sequoia. That practice is dangerous in its own right, and issuing a stern warning is certainly appropriate, but what Apple did at the time was force us to confirm these permissions every week and every time we restarted our computers.

This approach was widely criticized as turning macOS into Microsoft Vista and imposing "a subscription you didn't buy and can't cancel." In my view, the occasional permission requests repeated on iPhone have already gone too far. For example, I have already granted Citymapper access to my location so it can provide navigation in the background; Apple, I really don't need you to ask me again whether I still want to do this.

For granting high-level access, there absolutely should be the strongest warning possible, but if someone chooses to do so, macOS must respect their decision. Thank you, but please do not force weekly or other periodic confirmations.
